passage: The temple fair in Sudha's kasba had been a long, hot day: the giant wheel broke down twice, her sandal strap snapped, and she spent an hour helping her uncle at the bangle stall. That night, on the charpai, she scrolled through sixty photos and chose three. A selfie with cotton candy, lit gold by the sunset. The giant wheel from below, looking enormous. And a funny edit of her cousin Charu in a paper crown with cartoon sparkles, captioned "queen of the mela 👑". Within an hour, classmates from town commented: "so jealous", "best day ever?" Charu, lying beside her, read the comments aloud and snorted. "Best day ever? You cried about the sandal." Sudha grinned. "Nobody wants the sandal." Then she paused. "Do you mind the crown one?" Charu shook her head. "I love it. Keep it." Sudha put the phone away, still smiling, the snapped sandal under the charpai.

qa.q: How many photos did Sudha choose from the sixty?
qa.a: Sudha chose three of the sixty photos.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling while choosing the photos?
qa.a: Sudha seems happy and playful picking the bright moments, maybe a bit proud of the edits; the tiring parts like the snapped sandal weren't gone, just left out. 🙂

qa.q: What did Sudha get right about the photo of Charu?
qa.a: Sudha asked Charu whether she minded the crown edit before keeping it up, which respected Charu's say over her own image.

qa.q: How might the classmates see Sudha's day compared with Charu?
qa.a: The classmates saw a golden 'best day ever', while Charu, who was there, knew about the heat, the broken wheel and the sandal.

grounding: It shows a teenager curating fair photos and edits to present a fun, glowing self, while the full day was more mixed than the posts.

passage:
Saturday. Helping Dolma clean her room, Eshaan picked a faded bus ticket off her mirror. "Siliguri to Kalimpong, 2022? This is rubbish. Or," he wiggled his eyebrows, "is it from someone?" Dolma snatched it back and tucked it into the mirror frame again. "Leave it." He shrugged and dropped the teasing, but he noticed she didn't throw away anything else from that trip either.
Tuesday. At dinner he asked, without the eyebrows this time, "What's the ticket, really?" Dolma was quiet, then said, "First trip I made alone, to see Momo-la before she got too sick. I was so scared of missing the stop that I held the ticket the whole way." Eshaan put down his spoon.
The next Sunday. Eshaan came home from the market with a small wooden frame, the cheap kind. "For the ticket," he said, pretending it was no big deal. Dolma put it on her desk, where she could see it every morning.

qa.q: What route was printed on the ticket?
qa.a: It was Siliguri to Kalimpong, 2022.

qa.q: Why did Dolma snatch the ticket back?
qa.a: Dolma felt protective and a bit stung by the teasing, because the ticket held a tender, sad memory of Momo-la; it could also have been embarrassment at Eshaan guessing out loud.

qa.q: What changed when Eshaan asked the second time?
qa.a: Eshaan asked without teasing and just listened, which let Dolma share the real meaning instead of shutting him out.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been feeling when he put down his spoon?
qa.a: Eshaan was probably moved and a little sorry for calling it rubbish, which is why he later brought a frame for it.

grounding: It shows a teenager keeping a ticket stub that stands for a relationship, and curiosity rather than assumption revealing what it means.

passage: I'm Lavanya, and I share a room with Indu-didi, so I notice things. Since the summer she has been taking twenty selfies before school and deleting nineteen. She runs the filter that makes skin look like glass, then frowns at her real face in the mirror, as if the mirror got it wrong. On Monday she changed her kurta three times and missed the bus. On Wednesday she said she looked "disgusting" in the class photo. I thought she looked like Indu. I don't know what goes on in her head; I only see the outside. That evening I told Amma about the deleted selfies. Amma didn't lecture. She sat on Didi's bed and said, "Wear what you like, change your hair, all of it is your choice. None of it is what you're worth." Didi rolled her eyes, but she didn't leave the room. Amma kept checking in, and on Friday she took Didi for a walk, just the two of them.

qa.q: How many selfies does Indu take before school?
qa.a: Indu takes twenty selfies before school and deletes nineteen.

qa.q: What might Indu be feeling when she frowns at the mirror?
qa.a: Indu seems unhappy and self-conscious, comparing her real face with the glassy filtered one; since Lavanya only sees the outside, it might also be ordinary morning stress.

qa.q: How did Amma support Indu?
qa.a: Amma didn't lecture, told Indu that clothes and hair are her choice but not her worth, and kept checking in, taking her for a walk on Friday.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see Indu in the class photo?
qa.a: To Lavanya, Indu just looked like Indu, not 'disgusting', which shows how differently Indu was seeing herself.

grounding: It shows a teenager comparing herself with filtered images and over-controlling clothes, and a parent stressing presentation as a choice, not a measure of worth, while watching over time.

passage: In the kasba's government school, the cricket nets were just a torn fishing net strung between two neem trees. Yash had stripped to his vest for batting practice, and the white thread across his shoulder showed. Rinku, new from the city, pointed. "Your parents make you wear that? Mine never would." Yash tapped it. "Nobody makes me. I asked for the ceremony. My grandfather tied it." He shrugged. "Some days it's prayer. Some days I forget it's there." Imran, padding up, grinned. "Don't look at me next. Yes, it's a cap. On Fridays I wear it for namaz. Other days it's because Abba says the sun will fry my brain." Rinku laughed, then went red. "Sorry. I thought it all meant the same thing for everyone." "Ask," said Yash, "and we'll tell you." Imran tossed Rinku the ball. "Now bowl. That's the only tradition here."

qa.q: Who tied Yash's thread?
qa.a: His grandfather tied it.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Rinku asked if his parents made him wear it?
qa.a: Yash seemed calm and a little amused, maybe slightly defensive since he said nobody makes him; the thread carries mixed meanings for him, prayer some days and habit on others.

qa.q: What is a better way for Rinku to handle this next time?
qa.a: Ask what the item means to that person instead of guessing, as Yash suggested, since the same thread or cap can mean faith, family or habit.

qa.q: How did Rinku see the thread at first?
qa.a: Rinku assumed it was something parents force on children, and went red on realising it meant different things to different people.

grounding: It shows a sacred thread and a cap carrying faith, family and everyday meanings for different teenagers, and a newcomer learning not to assume.

passage: When Jeevan came home from the barber in Kushalnagar with bleached orange tips and a tiny silver stud in one ear, Ajji put down her coffee. "Who are you trying to be? Is it those boys at the bus stand?" Jeevan's ears burned around the new stud. "It's just hair, Ajji." Tenzin, who had come along from the settlement to watch, shifted by the door. "Mine was green last year," he offered. "It washed out. My amala survived." Ajji didn't laugh. That evening Jeevan's father pulled an old album from the cupboard and put it on the table without a word. There he was in college, hair down to his shoulders and a bead necklace. Ajji peered at it and finally laughed. "I thought you'd joined a drama company." "I was trying things," Appa said. "Then I stopped. He will too, or he won't. Either is fine." Jeevan kept the stud. The orange lasted two weeks.

qa.q: What did Jeevan come home with from the barber?
qa.a: Jeevan came home with bleached orange tips and a tiny silver stud in one ear.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when Ajji asked 'Who are you trying to be?'
qa.a: Jeevan felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, ears burning, since the new look was just an experiment; there may also have been hurt at being linked to 'those boys'.

qa.q: How did Appa help settle the worry?
qa.a: He showed his own old college photo of trying out long hair and said Jeevan might stop or not and either was fine, treating the style as a trial, not trouble.

qa.q: What might Ajji have been worried about?
qa.a: Ajji seemed afraid the new look meant Jeevan was falling in with a bad crowd, until the old album showed it could simply be trying things.

grounding: It shows a teenager experimenting with hair and jewellery as trial and self-exploration, and a family seeing it is not proof of deeper trouble.

passage:
Sports teacher's note, after the inter-school final
Our Class 11 group sat in the east stand in maroon scarves. Bhupen, usually quiet in class, was on his feet from the first minute, leading the chant, face painted, hoarse by half-time. I've never seen him look so happy. When the referee gave a late penalty against us, the mood turned. Some older boys from another school started shoving at the railing, and a bottle flew. Bhupen was still chanting, pressed near the front. Rukmini tugged his sleeve and pointed at the exit. For a second he shook her off; then he looked around, saw the shoving and came with her. I was already moving our group to the side gate, and we left before the final whistle. On the bus Bhupen said, "I didn't even notice how close to the railing I was." Tomorrow I'll talk with the class about how crowds can carry us, and we'll agree a meeting point for next time.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do when the shoving started?
qa.a: Rukmini tugged his sleeve and pointed at the exit.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling while leading the chant?
qa.a: Bhupen was joyful and excited, feeling he belonged, on his feet and hoarse; being swept up may also have made him less aware of danger, as he admitted on the bus.

qa.q: What kept the group safe?
qa.a: Rukmini pointed to the exit, Bhupen chose to follow, and the teacher moved everyone to the side gate before the final whistle; a meeting point is planned for next time.

qa.q: What was it like for Rukmini to see Bhupen near the railing?
qa.a: Rukmini was likely worried for him and brave enough to tug his sleeve, even when he first shook her off.

grounding: It shows a teenager feeling belonging and heightened emotion in a cheering crowd, acting unlike his usual self, and leaving when things turn unsafe.

passage: The school courtyard in Nagpur was lined with clay diyas for Mr Deshmukh, the physics teacher who had died suddenly on Sunday. Class 10 stood in rows, holding marigolds. Kalyani was crying before the first lamp was lit, shoulders shaking, and kept whispering, "He wrote on my notebook last week." Avni stood beside her with a dry face and a strange hollow in her chest. She placed her flower by the photo, folded her hands, and felt nothing she could name. She wondered if something was wrong with her. Afterwards, on the steps, she admitted it in a low voice. "Everyone's crying and I just feel blank. Is that awful?" Kalyani wiped her face with her dupatta. "No. At our Nani's funeral my cousin didn't cry for a month, then cried over a biscuit." Avni almost smiled. They sat together until the diyas burned down, not talking much.

qa.q: What were Class 10 holding?
qa.a: Class 10 were holding marigolds.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling at the vigil?
qa.a: Avni felt numb and blank, a strange hollow in her chest, and then worried that something was wrong with her for not crying; the numbness can be its own form of grief.

qa.q: How did Kalyani help Avni?
qa.a: Kalyani didn't judge the blankness, shared a story showing grief can arrive late, and then simply sat with Avni until the diyas burned down.

qa.q: What was the vigil like for Kalyani?
qa.a: For Kalyani it was raw and tearful, remembering Mr Deshmukh writing on her notebook the week before.

grounding: It shows teenagers sharing grief at a school vigil with lamps and flowers, one crying and one feeling numb, both responses being real.

subtype: Affectionate and tender among friends and family [Regulating]
passage:
Warden's note, Sunday visiting hours
Preeti's mother, Chandrika, arrived at the gate with a steel tiffin and her arms already open. Preeti was standing with four girls from her floor. She gave a quick wave and a "Hi, Ma," and stepped back half a pace. Chandrika's arms came down slowly; her smile stayed on, a bit fixed. In the visitors' room, with the door half shut, it was different: Preeti leaned her whole head on her mother's shoulder and stayed there while Chandrika unpacked the parathas. When visiting ended, I walked Preeti back and mentioned, lightly, that her mother had looked a bit lost at the gate. Preeti went pink. "Everyone was watching. I'm not a baby." I said she didn't have to hug in public, but a few words might reach her mother. At lights-out Preeti showed me her phone: "sorry about the gate. missed you so much. the parathas were the best part of the week." Chandrika had replied with three hearts.

qa.q: What did Chandrika bring to the gate?
qa.a: Chandrika brought a steel tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Preeti step back at the gate?
qa.a: Preeti felt embarrassed about showing affection in front of the girls from her floor, not wanting to look like a baby; resting her head on her mother's shoulder later shows the warmth was still there.

qa.q: What did the warden suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: The warden said a public hug wasn't necessary but a few honest words might reach her mother, and Preeti's message about missing her repaired the moment.

qa.q: What was the gate moment like for Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika's arms came down slowly and her smile went fixed, so she likely felt hurt or a little lost until Preeti's message arrived.

grounding: It shows a teenager hiding affection in public while staying warm in private, and honest words keeping the bond alive.

passage: In their Mexico City school, Diego had called Yosef "Profesor" since the first week, because of the round glasses and the way Yosef explained football tactics with salt shakers. Yosef usually bowed and answered in a fake lecture voice, and the table cracked up. On Thursday the maths tests came back. Yosef's had a big red 5 on it, and he slid it into his bag fast. At lunch Diego, who hadn't noticed, called across the table, "Profesor! Explain to us the secrets of algebra!" A few people laughed. Yosef didn't bow. He smiled, but only with his mouth, and went back to his sandwich. Diego waited for the lecture voice. It didn't come. He looked at Yosef's bag, then at his face, and let it drop. "Actually, forget algebra. Explain why our team lost on Sunday." Yosef let out a breath and picked up a salt shaker. After school Diego asked, "The nickname. Still okay?" "Mostly," Yosef said. "Not today."

qa.q: What mark was on Yosef's maths test?
qa.a: It had a big red 5 on it.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when he smiled only with his mouth?
qa.a: Yosef was likely embarrassed and low after the bad test, so the nickname stung that day; it might also have been simple tiredness, which is why checking later mattered.

qa.q: What did Diego notice, and what did he do?
qa.a: Diego noticed the missing lecture voice and the tight smile, switched the topic to the match, and later asked whether the nickname was still okay. 👍

qa.q: What would have changed if Diego had kept pushing the joke?
qa.a: Yosef would likely have felt mocked about the grade in front of everyone, and the nickname could have turned from closeness into hurt.

grounding: It shows a nickname and banter signalling closeness, and a teenager reading the other boy's response to know when play should stop.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage: The day the Class 10 results came out, I went silent for about six hours. Seventy-one percent. Charu, my little sister, had got 94 in her Class 8 exams the same week, and Baba had already told the whole building. At dinner someone said, "Next time, more focus," and I pushed the plate away and said, "What's the point. I'm useless. There's no point in me." Charu stopped chewing. I remember Baba starting to answer with a lecture, and Maa putting her hand on his arm. She came to my room straight after, sat on the floor by my bed and said, "Anirban, I heard what you said, and I'm not leaving you alone with it tonight." She stayed until one. Before I slept, she called the helpline number the school gives out, with me beside her, and the next afternoon we saw the counsellor together. Charu slid a note under my door: "you're not useless, you taught me fractions." I still have it.

qa.q: What percentage did Anirban get?
qa.a: Anirban got seventy-one percent.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when pushing the plate away?
qa.a: Anirban felt crushed and hopeless, set beside Charu's 94 and stung by 'Next time, more focus'; saying 'no point in me' showed despair, not just disappointment.

qa.q: What did Maa do that mattered most?
qa.a: Maa stopped the lecture, stayed with Anirban that night instead of leaving it, called the helpline together before sleep and went with Anirban to the counsellor the next afternoon.

qa.q: What was it like for Charu to hear 'I'm useless'?
qa.a: Charu was startled, stopping mid-chew, and later tried to help by sliding a note saying Anirban had taught her fractions.

grounding: It shows a teenager going silent and calling themself useless after poor results, and a parent giving urgent, caring attention instead of a lecture.
